question text: A shop sells a used phone in instalments. What must its invoice contain?
ground truth: On the consumer's request, a clear invoice at no extra charge showing: supplier and shop name; date; price; type, essential features and warranty period; that the product is used (its condition); quantity; delivery date; signature or stamp. For instalments it must also show the total instalment amount, the actual annual interest rate and how it is calculated, the date interest starts, the number and value of instalments, the instalment period, penalties for default or late payment, the parties' rights over ownership during the period, and the consumer's acknowledgement of these terms. [Doc 6, Art. 4, pp. 14-15]
answer:
When selling a product in instalments, the supplier must provide the consumer with a clear and legible invoice—without any additional financial or non-financial charges—that contains both general transaction details and specific instalment information [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)]. 

The invoice must include:
* The supplier's name and commercial shop name [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The date of the transaction or contract [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The price of the product [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The type of product, its essential characteristics, and the warranty period [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* A statement that the product is used (since it is a used phone) [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The quantity of the product by number or weight [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The delivery date of the product [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The signature or stamp of the supplier or their legal representative [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].

Additionally, for instalment sales, the supplier must comply with the Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law and its regulations, and the invoice must set out these extra details:
* The total instalment amount [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The actual annual interest rate and how it is calculated [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The date from which interest starts to be calculated [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The number of instalments and the value of each instalment [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The instalment period/duration [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The penalties imposed on the consumer for defaulting or delaying instalment payments [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* The rights and obligations of both contracting parties regarding the ownership of the product and its disposal during the instalment period [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
* A confirmation that the consumer has reviewed and accepted these additional details [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].

question text: A shop advertised a television at a set price in a newspaper, then charged a higher price at the till. Which obligations does this breach and what penalty does the order refer to?
ground truth: Shops that announce retail prices must keep to them and must not manipulate them, especially at payment. Anyone advertising goods at a set price in newspapers or on roads must ensure the advertised price is actual and matches reality. Violators face the penalties in Decree-Law No. 18 of 1975 (as amended by Decree-Law No. 11 of 1977), as well as closure of the shop where the manipulation took place. [Doc 8, Art. 1-3, p. 7]
answer:
A shop that advertises a television at a set price in a newspaper and then charges a higher price at the till breaches the obligation that any person who advertises a good or provides a service at a specific price—whether through newspapers, street advertisements, or public roads—must ensure the advertised price is actual, matches reality, and is free from any methods of manipulation affecting consumers [Ministerial Order 14/2008, Article 2 (p. 7)]. Store owners and factories announcing retail prices must strictly adhere to those announced prices and avoid any price manipulation, especially when the goods are being paid for at the till [Ministerial Order 14/2008, Article 1 (p. 7)]. 

Regarding penalties, the relevant ministerial order refers to the penalties stipulated in Decree-Law No. 18 of 1975 on determining and controlling prices (as amended by Decree-Law No. 11 of 1977), while also taking into account the penalty of closing the commercial establishment where the price manipulation took place [Ministerial Order 14/2008, Article 3 (p. 7)].

question text: How long does a supplier have to provide spare parts and maintenance after a consumer asks, and when is it released from this duty?
ground truth: Within at most 15 working days of the request. The parties may agree a specific period in writing. The supplier is released if it notifies the consumer in writing that the parts are unavailable and the consumer agrees. [Doc 6, Art. 16, p. 18; Doc 4, Art. 9, p. 6]
answer:
A supplier must provide necessary spare parts and maintenance within a maximum of 15 working days from the date of the consumer's request, though the supplier and consumer may also agree in writing on a different period [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 16 (p. 18)]. 

The supplier is released from this duty if they notify the consumer in writing that spare parts are unavailable and the consumer agrees to this in writing [Law 35/2012 (EN), Article 9 (p. 6); Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 16 (p. 18)].

question text: How did the Education index change between August and September 2025 and from then to August 2026, and what does iGA's method say about how often education prices are collected and their weight?
ground truth: It rose 2.8% from 108.41 to 111.4 in September 2025 and stayed at 111.4 every month to August 2026. iGA's method lists education, 8.6% of the basket weight, under annual price collection. [Dataset 1: code 10; Doc 9, section 5.3, pp. 7-8]
answer:
Between August and September 2025, the national Education index rose 2.8%, moving from an index level of 108.4 in August 2025 to 111.4 in September 2025. From September 2025 to August 2026, the index did not change, remaining at 111.4. (Percentage changes are the group's own calculations from iGA index numbers.)

According to iGA's CPI methodology, education prices are collected annually, and the education group accounts for 8.6% of the total weight of the CPI basket [iGA CPI Sep 2023, excerpt 1 (p. 8)].

question text: A customer changes their mind about a jacket bought yesterday that has no fault. Must the shop exchange it or give a refund?
ground truth: No, unless the shop's own policy offers it, in which case the shop must keep to that policy. The legal right to exchange or refund applies only where goods have a defect or fault or do not conform to the approved specifications or the purpose of the contract. The Ministry's guidance lists a change of mind, finding the item cheaper elsewhere, a defect the consumer was told of at purchase, and damage from misuse as cases with no refund or replacement. [Doc 10, PDF pp. 7-8; Doc 6, Art. 14, pp. 17-18]
answer:
No, the shop is not required to give a refund or exchange if a customer simply changes their mind and the item has no fault [Know Your Right (MOIC guidance), excerpt 1 (p. 8)]. 

According to consumer guidance, a consumer should not expect a refund or replacement if they change their mind, did not benefit from using the item, find it cheaper elsewhere, were notified of defects at purchase, or if the item is damaged by misuse [Know Your Right (MOIC guidance), excerpt 1 (p. 8)]. Refunds and replacements are legally required when goods have a defect, do not conform to approved specifications, or do not suit the purpose for which the contract was entered into [Know Your Right (MOIC guidance), excerpt 1 (p. 8)]. (Note that this guidance dates from 2016 and predates Law No. 28 of 2026.)
